analysis.one_liner: Exempts direct sellers and real estate agents from federal minimum wage and overtime rules.
analysis.headline: The House Labor Committee approved the bill 19-16 and placed it on the House calendar, but the full House has not voted.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill writes direct sellers and qualified real estate agents out of the Fair Labor Standards Act's definition of "employee." Workers who are employees under that law must be paid at least the federal minimum wage and, when they work more than 40 hours a week, overtime pay. The bill would say these workers do not count, no matter how many hours they put in or how little they earn.
analysis.who_benefits: Direct-selling companies (including multilevel marketing firms) and real estate brokerages, whose commissioned salesforces could never claim federal minimum wage or overtime against them, and no longer face the risk that courts or the Labor Department would reclassify them as employees. Some sellers and agents themselves also benefit from the flexibility and tax treatment of independent status.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Direct-selling firms and real estate brokerages

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the FLSA so that a direct seller or qualified real estate agent, as defined in tax law, is not an employee, which means no minimum wage or overtime obligation applies to them.

Writing the exclusion into the statute itself gives companies that pay only on commission certainty that they owe no hourly wages regardless of how many hours a seller works or how low the seller's net earnings fall.

analysis.who_pays: The workers themselves: direct sellers, many of whom net little after their own costs, and real estate agents who put in long hours for small commission checks, who would lose the federal wage floor and overtime as protections they could ever claim.
analysis.who_pays_short: Commissioned direct sellers and real estate agents

drawbacks.text: Workers covered by the bill would have no federal right to be paid at least minimum wage or to receive overtime for hours beyond 40 a week.

The exclusion would be permanent federal law, so it would foreclose future Department of Labor rules or court decisions that might otherwise classify these workers as employees with wage and hour rights.
The bill does not create any new benefit for workers; it only removes an existing legal protection that could otherwise be claimed in a lawsuit over unpaid hours.

A supporter's honest case is that commission-based agents and sellers set their own hours and often earn well, so hourly wage rules fit poorly; the strongest answer is that this does not describe the many direct sellers who earn little or nothing once their own expenses are counted, and they are the ones who lose the wage floor.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For well-paid real estate agents, losing minimum wage and overtime rights costs almost nothing, since they are paid by commission and some value independent status. The cost falls on the lower-earning end of the covered workforce, especially direct sellers, who are often paid nothing but commissions and bear their own selling costs; for them the federal wage floor is the main protection against effectively working below minimum wage. The bill's clearest financial gain goes to the companies, not the workers.

outcome.mechanism: The House Education and Workforce Committee voted 19-16 to send the bill to the full House and it was placed on the House calendar, but no floor vote has been scheduled yet.

narrative.text: Representative Kevin Kiley introduced the bill in May 2025, joined by Representative Henry Cuellar, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.
The committee held a markup session on September 17, 2025, and ordered the bill reported with amendments by a vote of 19 to 16.
The committee formally reported the bill to the House on February 11, 2026, with a written report, and it was placed on the Union Calendar, which is the queue for bills awaiting House floor action.
The bill carries 31 cosponsors, 11 of 216 House Democrats and 20 of 223 House Republicans.
As of the latest action, the full House has not taken a vote on the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the direct-selling and real estate brokerage industries are ahead: their salesforces' independent-contractor status has advanced toward being written permanently into federal wage law, while the workers involved have gained nothing new and would give up wage-hour protections if it passes.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Direct-selling and brokerage companies, so far

sides.party_line_note: The committee vote split 19-16, in line with the Republican majority, but the cosponsor list is bipartisan: 11 of 216 House Democrats and 20 of 223 House Republicans signed on.

industries.note: These companies rely on salesforces paid only by commission, and the bill would relieve them of any minimum wage or overtime obligation no matter how much a seller nets. The companies' saving is the worker's lost wage floor.

Brokerages would gain certainty that agents are independent contractors under federal wage law, cutting off wage-and-hour claims. Many real estate agents are well paid by commission and prefer independent status, so the loss to workers in this sector is comparatively small.

industries.industry: Commissioned direct sellers and real estate agents
industries.note: These workers would permanently lose the federal minimum wage and overtime protections, though some agents value the flexibility of independent status.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits on the House calendar awaiting a floor vote. Bipartisan committee-reported bills like this are often brought up under a fast-tracked procedure that needs a two-thirds majority, so a vote this session is plausible; if the House never schedules one, the bill dies when this Congress ends in January 2027.
